subject: Clarification: session vs. per-token accounting for legacy pilot
messages:
From: Emma Johnson <emma.johnson@greenline.com>
To: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@greenline.com
Date: Sun, 9 May 2027 09:14:00 -0700
Subject: Billing units — how do legacy sessions map to tokens?

Hi Rafael,

Thanks for the product walkthrough yesterday. Our legal and procurement teams are digging into the pricing attachment you sent and we hit a point that needs clarification: Greenline has an existing 'session-based' vendor that charges per-session with a 1,000-token context budget and a monthly minimum. For the Redwood pilot we expect a mix of long-context analysis runs (~6k tokens) and lots of short lookups (~200 tokens).

Can you explain how Redwood would meter and bill these workloads under the pilot:
- If a single user opens a long analysis that uses 6k tokens, is that billed as 6k tokens or as multiple session windows?
- Are there minimums applied per API call, per conversation, or per "session"?
- What rounding rules apply to partial tokens/streams and to streaming responses?

Procurement also asked whether we can get a simple worked example for a week with 3 long analyses (6k tokens each) plus 1,200 short lookups (200 tokens each). We would like to map that back to the monthly pilot invoice.

I've attached a small sample of expected usage.

Appreciate a clear mapping so we can sign off internally.

Best,
Emma
Senior Data Platform Manager
Greenline Analytics

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.com>
To: Emma Johnson <emma.johnson@greenline.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.com, ben_carter@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 10 May 2027 11:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Billing units — how do legacy sessions map to tokens?

Hi Emma — thanks, and great questions. I pulled together a short explainer + worked example below. Happy to hop on a quick call if you want to walk the spreadsheet together.

Summary answers first:
- Redwood meters per-token. Long analyses using 6k tokens are billed for the full token count consumed (6,000 tokens). We do not silently split into multiple "sessions" for billing purposes; each request's token usage is counted.
- There are two important aggregation layers that affect how that maps to invoices: (1) per-request rounding quantum (we round to 8-token granularity for per-call metering), and (2) conversation-level rollups used for discounts/minimums (we aggregate calls into conversation buckets for the monthly invoice where applicable).
- Minimums are applied at the contract line-item level (e.g., pilot SKUs can have a monthly minimum consumption commitment). We can also offer per-customer smoothing credits for noisy short-call patterns.

Worked example (your ask):
- 3 long analyses × 6,000 tokens = 18,000 tokens raw
  - Per-call rounding to 8-token quantum -> each 6,000 rounded to nearest multiple of 8 is still 6,000 (no change)
- 1,200 short lookups × 200 tokens = 240,000 tokens raw
  - Each 200-token call rounds to 200 (already multiple of 8); aggregated total 240,000
- Total raw tokens = 258,000 -> billed tokens after per-call rounding: 258,000

Invoice aggregation and minimums:
- If the pilot contract has a monthly minimum of 250k tokens, you'd meet it (258k billed) and be charged the actual billed tokens at the negotiated per-token rate.
- If you fell below the monthly minimum (e.g., 160k billed), we'll either apply the minimum as a charge or convert the difference into a credit that you can apply to future months (we can negotiate which outcome for the pilot).

Streaming: each emitted token is metered; for streaming responses we still apply the same per-token counting and per-call rounding (for the request/response pair).

Edge cases and exceptions we typically handle on pilots:
- Very long interactive sessions where kv-cache/prefix reuse reduces per-token cost. We can set up a "conversation bucket" to meter a set of requests under one logical session and optionally apply a separate discount profile.
- If you have large batched requests that are split for execution, billing corresponds to the original logical request token count, not the internal execution chunks.

Next steps:
1) If this mapping looks acceptable, I can produce a one-page appendix for the SOW that states the rounding quantum, monthly minimum handling, and the exception process.
2) Marissa (cc) can propose a pilot concession if you need to hit an internal procurement threshold for approval.

Rafael
Sales Engineer
Redwood Inference

If Greenline wants the alternative of a hard monthly minimum with a reduced per-token rate instead, we can draft that as option B in the SOW. Which does procurement prefer: (A) credit-first ramp or (B) reduced unit price with a hard commit?
